title: Substitution or elimination: explain the change in product ratio
asks: The same substrate gives different amounts of substitution and elimination with two different reagents. Explain, naming the reactions.

know.h: Substitution and elimination compete. The same anion can attack the carbon that carries the leaving group ({{SN2}}) or remove a hydrogen from the carbon next to it ({{E2}}). A carbocation can add a nucleophile ({{SN1}}) or lose a neighbouring hydrogen ({{E1}}).
A better base favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}. A better nucleophile favors {{SN2}} over {{E2}}.

Judge base strength by the {{pKa}} of the conjugate acid. Strong bases: {{HO-}} (water 15.7), {{CH3O-}} (methanol 15.5), {{CH3CH2O-}} (ethanol 15.9), {{(CH3)3CO-}} (tert-butyl alcohol 17). Weak bases: {{HS-}} ({{H2S}} 10 in lecture), acetate (acetic acid 4), {{I-}} (HI -10).
Judge nucleophilicity by the lecture table (relative {{SN2}} rate): {{HS-}} 126,000; {{I-}} 80,000; {{HO-}} 16,000; {{N3-}} 8,000; acetate 630; water and methanol 1.
A secondary halide is where the reagent decides. A weak base that is a good nucleophile gives mostly {{SN2}}. A strong base gives mostly {{E2}}, with a little {{SN2}}.

The substrate changes the ratio. More branching on the carbon with the leaving group, or on the carbon next to it, slows {{SN2}} (ethyl 0.033, isobutyl 0.003, isopropyl 0.00083, tert-butyl 0) and so favors {{E2}}. Methyl: only {{SN2}}. Primary: mostly {{SN2}}. Secondary with a strong base: mostly {{E2}}. Tertiary with a strong base: only {{E2}}.

A bulky base favors elimination. tert-Butoxide is a strong base and a poor nucleophile: it cannot reach the carbon, but it can reach a hydrogen on the outside of the molecule. It gives {{E2}} even with a primary halide.
A methyl halide cannot eliminate: there is no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon. This is why an ether is best made from the alkoxide of the bulky group and a methyl or primary halide.
High temperature favors elimination. For tert-butyl bromide in water, {{SN1}} (the alcohol) is favored at lower temperature and {{E1}} (the alkene) at high temperature.

With no strong base, a tertiary halide reacts through its carbocation ({{SN1}} and {{E1}}). Adding a strong base changes the mechanism to {{E2}}: tert-butyl bromide gives the alcohol in water alone, but only the alkene with NaOH.

Skill: name both reactions and draw both products. A full answer says which mechanism makes the substitution product, which makes the elimination product, and which property of the reagent, substrate or temperature tips the balance.

method: Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group: this tells you which mechanisms are possible at all.
Say what is being changed between the two experiments: the reagent, the substrate, or the temperature.
If the reagent changes, compare base strength (the {{pKa}} of each conjugate acid) and bulk, and compare nucleophilicity.
If the substrate changes, compare how hindered the carbon is and whether a hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon exists.
Name the substitution reaction and the elimination reaction ({{SN2}} and {{E2}} with an anionic reagent, {{SN1}} and {{E1}} in a neutral protic solvent), and draw the product of each.
Finish with one sentence that links cause to result, for example: stronger base, more {{E2}}.

pitfalls.h: Explaining the change without naming the reactions. The question asks for the names: {{SN2}} and {{E2}}, or {{SN1}} and {{E1}}.
Calling acetate or {{HS-}} a strong base because it has a negative charge. Use the {{pKa}} of the conjugate acid.
Using {{SN1}} and {{E1}} for a secondary halide with an anionic reagent. A good nucleophile or strong base reacts before the halide can ionize.
Saying only that one reagent is the stronger nucleophile. The balance depends on base strength as well: ethoxide is a fair nucleophile but a much stronger base than acetate.
Forgetting that a methyl halide cannot eliminate and a tertiary halide cannot do {{SN2}}.
